title: How to talk about your experience
sub: Answering “have you done this in production” with a template — what, how much, why not further — and three phrases that show you have really done it
cards/0/body:
“Have you used Jobs and Burst in production?” is not a yes-or-no question. The interviewer checks three things: did you measure, do you understand the cost of the decision, and are you honest. “Yes, everything we had was on jobs” fails all three: the very next question, “how much did it give?”, leaves you without numbers.

A strong answer is one concrete 40–60 second story in three parts:

What. The task, the scale, and how you found the bottleneck — a Profiler marker, milliseconds, the device.

How much you got. Before → after, in milliseconds, main thread and workers separately, and how you measured.

Why not further. What stopped you: the next bottleneck was elsewhere, a rewrite cost more than it would gain, the frame budget already fit. This part is what sets a senior apart: they know where to stop.
cards/0/flow/0: What: task, scale, how you found it
cards/0/flow/1: How much: before → after, how measured
cards/0/flow/2: Why not further: what stopped you
cards/1/body:
This is a model of the form, not someone’s story to retell: the candidate, the project and the numbers are invented for this example. Build your own answer only on your own measurements.

What. “A mobile strategy game had about 3,000 units, and the neighbour search for collision avoidance ran in each unit’s Update. I wrapped it in a marker, and the Profiler in a development build on our test Android device showed about 7 ms per frame there.”

What I did. “I gathered the positions into a Persistent NativeArray<float3>, the neighbour grid into a NativeParallelMultiHashMap, and the search itself became an IJobParallelFor with [BurstCompile]. Schedule in Update, ScheduleBatchedJobs right after, Complete in LateUpdate.”

How much. “Under 0.5 ms was left on the main thread — gathering data and applying results; the job itself took about 1 ms on the workers. Same marker, same build, same device.”

Why not further. “After that the frame was bound by rendering, not logic. Moving the units to Entities would have meant rewriting animation and the UI links — not worth it for the remaining millisecond. With several times more units I would have revisited it.”
cards/2/q: Put the parts of a “have you done this in production” answer in order.
cards/2/items/0: Task and scale: what system, how many objects, which platform
cards/2/items/1: How you found it: a Profiler marker, how many ms per frame
cards/2/items/2: What you did: job type, Burst, data layout, where Schedule and Complete go
cards/2/items/3: How much you got: before → after, and how you measured
cards/2/items/4: Why you went no further: the next bottleneck or the cost of a rewrite
cards/2/explain: Context first, so the numbers mean something; then the solution; then the result with how it was measured; and finally the boundary — where and why you stopped.
cards/3/body:
“How much you got” without a method is not a number. A performance-minded interviewer will ask where you measured.

Not in the Editor without caveats. The Editor runs safety checks, the Jobs Debugger and leak detection, and by default Burst compiles asynchronously: for the first frames your code runs as plain managed C#. For Editor measurements turn on Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation and let it warm up. More reliable is a development build on the target device: safety checks are unavailable in builds, and the numbers are closer to what a player sees.

The same conditions. Same marker, same scene, same device before and after. Main thread and workers separately: a 1 ms job on the workers and a 0.1 ms wait on the main thread are different things.

If you have not done it in production, say so, then tell what you did do: “not in production; in my own project I moved this loop, measured, it was X, it became Y; in a real project I expect it to hit Z.” Invented experience falls apart on the second follow-up, while an honest test bench with numbers is valued.
cards/4/q: What makes an answer to “have you done this in production” stronger? Select all that apply.
cards/4/options/0: Before → after numbers and what you measured on: device, build type, marker
cards/4/options/1: The reason you stopped: the next bottleneck or the cost of a rewrite
cards/4/options/2: An honest “not in production, but in my own project I did this and measured that”
cards/4/options/3: “Burst speeds code up 10–100 times” with no measurements of your own
cards/4/options/4: Editor numbers with asynchronous Burst compilation, no caveats
cards/4/options/5: Listing every API you know instead of one story
cards/4/explain: A strong answer can be checked: numbers with a method, the boundary of the decision, honesty about the scale of your experience. Borrowed multipliers, raw Editor numbers and a list of APIs without a story show you never measured yourself.
cards/5/q: You have not used Jobs in production, but you built a practice project. Which answer is better?
cards/5/options/0: “Not in production. In my own project I moved the movement of 100,000 points into a Burst job and measured in a development build: it was this much, it became that much. In a real project I expect to hit the sync with GameObjects”
cards/5/options/1: “Yes, of course, everything we had was on jobs” — they cannot check anyway
cards/5/options/2: “No” — and stop there, so as not to say too much
cards/5/options/3: Retell a conference talk as your own experience
cards/5/explain: Honesty plus specifics: what you did, how you measured and where you expect trouble. Invented experience breaks on the follow-ups, and a bare “no” throws away the chance to show what you can do.
cards/6/title: “Profile first, then Burst the hot loop”
cards/6/body:
The meaning: measure first, then Burst. You do not rewrite everything as jobs; you find the hot loop in the Profiler — the spot where the milliseconds really go — and move exactly that into a Burst job.

Once you say it, be ready for the follow-ups:

“How did you find it?” — a ProfilerMarker around the suspicious code, the Hierarchy and Timeline views of the CPU Usage module, milliseconds per frame on the target device.

“What if there is no hot spot and the time is smeared?” — then Burst is not the cure: it is a question of architecture, of the number of objects, sometimes of moving to Entities.

“How much did it give?” — your numbers from the template.
cards/7/title: “SoA so Burst can vectorize — and I check it in the Burst Inspector”
cards/7/body:
The meaning: you lay data out as SoA — one array per field — because then neighbouring values of one field are contiguous, and Burst can process 4 or 8 of them with one SIMD instruction. With AoS — an array of structs — the loop drags every field through the cache, and the value it needs sits at a stride of the struct size.

And you check rather than hope: Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector, option “Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed”. mulss is a scalar multiply, one float at a time; mulps/vmulps are packed, 4 or 8 at a time.

Follow-ups: “What blocks vectorization?” — branches in the loop body (fixed with math.select), possible pointer aliasing ([NoAlias]; a job’s container fields are treated as non-overlapping by default), calls that do not inline. “What do you look for in the Inspector?” — packed instructions in the hot loop.
cards/8/body:
The meaning: Schedule() as soon as the input is ready, JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() right after, and Complete() as late as possible, when you actually need the result. The classic is Schedule in Update, Complete in LateUpdate.

How to check it: in the Profiler Timeline a main-thread wait for jobs shows up as a WaitForJobGroupID marker. If it is long at your Complete(), the job started late or Complete() sits too early.

Follow-ups: “What if you need the result sooner?” — push Complete() down as far as you can, or deliberately use last frame’s result at the cost of one frame of latency. “And in Entities?” — there state.Dependency does it: systems chain jobs onto each other with no Complete().
cards/9/q: Match each phrase with the follow-up question it invites
cards/9/pairs/0/1: How did you find the hot loop, and what did it cost?
cards/9/pairs/2/1: How can you tell from the assembly that a loop is vectorized?
cards/9/pairs/3/1: What will the Timeline show if Complete comes right after Schedule?
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “How much did Burst give you?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/10/options/0: “The neighbour search took 7 ms on the main thread. Now the main thread spends under 0.5 ms and the job itself about 1 ms on the workers. Same marker, development build, test device”
cards/10/options/3: “I didn’t measure, but the code looks faster”
cards/10/explain: Concrete milliseconds, main thread and workers apart, and the measurement conditions — that is the answer. “Ten times” is someone else’s multiplier, and “FPS went up” is not about this loop. And be ready for the follow-up: that is Burst and parallelism together; to name Burst’s share alone, you need a separate measurement of the same job without [BurstCompile].
cards/11/body:
This is a 5–10 minute task, and it is worth doing in writing. Fill in the template with your own story: only what you did and measured yourself. Where you have no numbers, write honestly that you did not measure, and think about how you will measure it in the practice at the end of the course.

Then say the answer out loud and time it: 40–60 seconds. Work in one of the three phrases where it is really about you, and check that you are ready for its follow-ups.

If you have no production experience, use the bottom part of the template. After the Unity practice in the course finale you will have numbers of your own for it.
cards/11/code:
What
  <the system and the scale: how many objects, platform>
Found it
  <Profiler marker, ms per frame, device, build type>
Did
  <job type, Burst, data layout, where Schedule and Complete go>
Got
  <before → after in ms; main thread and workers; how measured>
Why not further
  <the next bottleneck, the cost of a rewrite, the risk>
Next
  <what you would do with more time or twice the objects>

If you have not done it in production
  “Not in production. In my own project I did …”
  “I measured …: it was …, it became ….”
  “In a real project I expect it to hit …”
